question:
Patient note:
A 78-year-old retired shipyard engineer was referred to the internal-medicine clinic by his new primary physician for a comprehensive review of comorbid conditions before scheduling elective cataract extraction, as he has not had a full medical evaluation in nearly two years. He reports that five years ago he awoke with crushing substernal pressure radiating into the left arm and jaw while raking leaves; paramedics transported him to a community hospital where emergent coronary angiography demonstrated an occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery that was treated with a drug-eluting stent. He recalls spending three nights in the cardiac step-down unit, completing dual antiplatelet therapy for a year, and subsequently remaining on low-dose aspirin, high-intensity atorvastatin, and a low-dose beta-blocker without recurrent chest discomfort, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower-extremity edema. He performs most household tasks, trims hedges, and walks his dog one-half mile daily, having to pause only for mild knee arthritis rather than shortness of breath. He denies calf cramping with ambulation, non-healing foot ulcers, or temperature asymmetry of the extremities, and his last ankle–brachial index measured at a health-screening fair was 1.04 bilaterally. He has never experienced transient speech difficulty, unilateral weakness, facial asymmetry, or visual field changes, and his family remarks that his memory remains sharp: he manages online banking and completes crossword puzzles each morning. Pulmonary history is notable only for seasonal allergic rhinitis; he has never smoked, never carried inhalers, and has had no episodes of bronchitis or emphysema. Gastrointestinal review reveals no dyspepsia, epigastric pain relieved by food or antacids, hematemesis, melena, or prior endoscopy. Six years ago routine serologies showed isolated hepatitis B core antibody positivity, and follow-up elastography last autumn yielded a liver stiffness of 6.3 kPa without nodularity; alanine aminotransferase today is 48 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 46 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 94 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1—values he has been told reflect early chronic hepatic involvement without portal hypertension. Endocrine review notes that fasting plasma glucose has hovered between 102 and 118 mg/dL for the past decade, and a hemoglobin A1c last quarter was 6.2 %, so he adheres to a Mediterranean-style diet, measures his blood sugar once weekly to “keep an eye on it,” and has never required metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin; he reports no visual blurring, paresthesias, renal colic, or prior episodes of hypoglycemia. Renal function, however, has slowly deteriorated: serum creatinine two years ago was 1.9 mg/dL and today is 2.4 mg/dL with blood urea nitrogen 44 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL/min/1.73 m². He has no history of nephrolithiasis, obstructive uropathy, or protein-spilling glomerular disease, takes lisinopril 10 mg daily for long-standing hypertension, avoids nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories, and reports stable morning weights with good urine output. There is no personal or family history of hematologic or solid-organ malignancy, lymphadenopathy, night sweats, or unintended weight loss, and recent prostate-specific antigen was 1.4 ng/mL. He tested negative for human immunodeficiency virus on admission to a rehabilitation facility after hip replacement eight years ago and has had no risky behaviors since. Current medications include aspirin 81 mg, metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, lisinopril as noted, vitamin D3 for osteopenia documented on a screening DEXA scan, and occasional acetaminophen for mechanical knee pain; he takes no proton-pump inhibitors, corticosteroids, anticoagulants, or immunosuppressants. He drinks one glass of red wine with dinner three nights per week and quit chewing tobacco four decades earlier. Vital signs in clinic: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 126/68 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 62 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. He appears lean with a body mass index of 24 kg/m², is conversant, and ambulates unassisted. Cardiovascular examination reveals a well-healed left groin puncture scar, normal S1 and S2, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruits. Jugular venous pulsation is estimated at 6 cm H₂O, and there are no rales or wheezes over clear lungs. Abdomen is soft and non-tender; the liver edge is palpable 1 cm below the costal margin, smooth, and non-nodular, and there is no splenomegaly, ascites, or shifting dullness. Extremities demonstrate warm skin, symmetric 2+ radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses, no clubbing or cyanosis, and no edema. Neurologic testing shows intact cranial nerves II–XII, full strength throughout, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and steady tandem gait. Laboratory panel beyond those noted shows hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.2 × 10⁹/L, platelets 212 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, calcium 9.1 mg/dL, fasting triglycerides 138 mg/dL, LDL 71 mg/dL, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein 1.8 mg/L. A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained today shows normal sinus rhythm at 64 beats/min with Q waves in leads V1–V3 consistent with the prior anterior infarction but no new ST-segment deviations or T-wave inversions. Chest radiograph demonstrates clear lung fields and normal cardiac silhouette. The patient seeks guidance on perioperative risk mitigation and ongoing management of progressive renal impairment in the context of otherwise stable cardiovascular, hepatic, and metabolic status.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Use the age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), adding age points to the weights of qualifying conditions at presentation.
- Age 78: the 70–79 age band contributes 3 points.
- Prior myocardial infarction: the anterior infarction treated with an LAD stent contributes 1 point. The stent adds no separate points.
- Mild chronic liver disease: early chronic hepatic involvement without portal hypertension contributes 1 point.
- Moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease: eGFR 26 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates stage 4 CKD, contributing 2 points.
- Other CCI conditions: 0 points. A1c 6.2% and fasting glucose 102–118 mg/dL indicate prediabetes, not diabetes. No heart failure, peripheral or cerebrovascular disease, dementia, chronic pulmonary disease, connective tissue disease, peptic ulcer, hemiplegia, malignancy, or AIDS is documented.
Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 0 = 7.
Final answer: 7
